facts.claim: "The Roses" is on Amber Run's Sunflower release, issued 13 February 2026 on Tripel.
Discogs credits "The Roses" as written by Amber Run with Josh Noble and Karl Zeigler, and produced by Kev Jones.
On the Sunflower picture-disc release, Discogs lists Tom Archer as mixer, Katie Tavini as mastering engineer and Glyn Daniels on drums. These are release-level credits, not specific to this track.
Melomaniacs reviewer says 'The Roses' is the darkest point of the Sunflower EP and is driven by obsession and imbalance.
The band said ahead of the EP's release that its songs are about family in all its forms: the one you're born into, the one you choose, and the people you love and lose.
The title track 'Sunflower' was written as a love letter to singer Joe Keogh's now-wife.
Amber Run are a Nottingham trio: Joe Keogh (vocals, guitar), Tom Sperring (bass) and Henry Wyeth (keyboards).
Amber Run formed in September 2012. Their debut album 5AM (2015) reached No. 36 in the UK, and they were signed to RCA after playing the 2013 Reading and Leeds festivals.
Their 2023 album How to Be Human was released on Tripel. Their 2014 single "I Found" has passed half a billion streams, helped by TikTok.

research.lineage: Amber Run sit in British indie-pop and indie-rock, in the tradition of emotive, anthemic, heart-on-sleeve songwriting that Last.fm places alongside Kodaline.

draft:
**The Roses** begins closer to a confession than a performance. Joe Keogh sings in a mid-range that's a little raw at the edges, half-speaking the lines, the way you'd explain something across a kitchen table rather than from a stage. Underneath, a clean electric guitar picks out a simple arpeggio. The bass sits low and the beat holds a steady, unhurried mid-tempo with a relaxed, almost sagging feel. The room is dry and the vocal is close-miked, so the voice has nowhere to hide. Then the song leans forward. A second, higher voice comes in, the groove starts to push, and the whole thing fills out without losing that cramped, intimate feel.

The pull between holding back and pushing out matters, because this is the hardest song on Sunflower. Ahead of the release, Amber Run said the EP's songs are about family in all its forms: the one you're born into, the one you choose, and the people you love and lose. The title track was written as a love letter to Keogh's now-wife. "The Roses" comes from the same garden but shows the thorns. Melomaniacs called it the darkest point on the record, a song driven by obsession and imbalance, and the sound fits that reading. A lopsided love rarely announces itself with a big chorus. It mutters and circles, in a level voice that keeps threatening to give, and it gets louder only when it can't stay contained anymore.

Amber Run come out of the British indie tradition of heart-on-sleeve, built-for-singalong songwriting, on the same shelf as Kodaline. The Nottingham trio formed in 2012: Keogh on vocals and guitar, Tom Sperring on bass, Henry Wyeth on keys. Their 2014 single "I Found" has passed half a billion streams, with a long second life helped along by TikTok, and its open-armed ache is what most listeners know them for. "The Roses" bends that formula. It keeps the emotional directness but trades the anthem's release for something tighter and more uneasy. The swell is still there, but it plays less like catharsis than pressure building in a small room.

The band wrote it with Josh Noble and Karl Zeigler. Kev Jones produced it, and it came out on Tripel, the label behind 2023's How to Be Human. Keeping it dry and close was the right call. Any reverb would have given the feeling somewhere to go, and the point is that it doesn't have anywhere.

It sticks because it lets you hear how calm someone can sound right up until the feeling they're describing stops fitting inside them.
